1.1: This all went down back in the days of King Ahasuerus—the same king who ruled over 127 provinces from India all the way to Ethiopia.
1.2: Back then, he was sittin' on his throne in the palace at Shushan, holdin' it down.
1.3: In the third year of his reign, he threw a big feast for all his officials and servants. All the powerful folks from Persia and Media showed up—the nobles and provincial leaders too.
1.4: He was flexin'—showin' off how rich he was and how majestic everything looked. That man kept it goin' for 180 days straight.
1.5: After that, he hosted another feast for everybody in Shushan, from the highest to the lowest, right in the courtyard of the palace garden. That one lasted 7 days.
1.6: The spot was decked out with white and blue curtains, tied with fancy linen cords hangin' on silver rods and marble columns. The couches? Made of gold and silver, sittin' on a floor that looked like a whole art piece—alabaster, turquoise, and black and white marble.
1.7: They was servin' drinks in gold cups—each one different from the next. And the royal wine? Flowin' heavy, like the king had no limits.
1.8: The king said nobody was required to drink if they ain't want to. He told his staff, 'Let folks sip how they want.'
1.9: Queen Vashti? She had her own thing goin' on. She was throwin' a feast for the women in the king's royal palace.
1.10: On the seventh day, after the king had a lil' too much wine and was feelin' real good, he told his seven eunuchs—Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas—
1.11: 'Go get Queen Vashti. Tell her to come through wearin' her crown so everybody can see how fine she is.' He really wanted to show her off.
1.12: But Vashti wasn't goin'. She straight up said no to the king's command. That made the king furious—he was heated.
1.13: So he called up the wise men who were known for knowin' the law and how things worked in the kingdom.
1.14: These were his go-to guys: Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan—the top seven princes of Persia and Media, who had VIP access to the king.
1.15: 'So what we supposed to do with Queen Vashti?' the king asked. 'She broke the royal order. What's the move according to the law?'
1.16: Memucan stood up and said, 'This ain't just about the king. Vashti just disrespected everybody—the princes, the people, the whole kingdom.'
1.17: 'Word gon' get out that the queen told the king no, and women everywhere gon' start gettin' bold, disrespectin' their men too.'
1.18: 'By tonight, all the noble women in Persia and Media gon' be tellin' their husbands what Vashti did. This thing gon' spread, and the whole kingdom gon' be outta order.'
1.19: 'If the king down with it, he should drop a royal decree—put it in writing so it can't be changed: Vashti can't come before the king no more. And her royal spot? Give that to someone better.'
1.20: 'Once the word gets out across the whole empire—and it's a big one—all the wives gon' respect their husbands, whether they big time or low key.'
1.21: The king and the princes liked what Memucan said. So the king did just that.
1.22: He sent letters out to every province, in their own language and writing, sayin' that every man should run his own house and speak his people's language.

2.1: After all that went down, and the king finally cooled off, he started thinkin' about Vashti—what she did and what had been decided about her.
2.2: His attendants came through like, 'Let's go find some fine young virgins for the king.'
2.3: 'Have officers in every province gather up all the baddest young virgins and bring 'em to Shushan, to the women's quarters. Put 'em under Hegai, the king's eunuch in charge of the ladies. Give 'em all the spa treatments they need.'
2.4: 'Then whichever girl the king likes most—she can take Vashti's place as queen.' This idea sounded real good to the king, so he went ahead with it.
2.5: Now in Shushan, there was this Jewish man named Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish—a Benjamite.
2.6: Kish had been taken from Jerusalem back when Jeconiah was king of Judah, and Nebuchadnezzar from Babylon scooped everybody up.
2.7: Mordecai was raisin' his cousin Hadassah—aka Esther—'cause she ain't have no mom or dad. The girl was fine and had a good heart. When her parents passed, Mordecai took her in like his own daughter.
2.8: So when the king's order got out and all the young women were gathered at Shushan under Hegai's care, Esther got caught up in that too. They brought her to the palace, right into Hegai's hands.
2.9: And Esther? She instantly stood out. Hegai liked her vibe, so he gave her the hookup—extra beauty products, special food, seven handpicked maids from the palace, and moved her into the best room in the women's section.
2.10: Esther ain't tell nobody she was Jewish or about her family. Mordecai had told her to keep that on the low.
2.11: And every single day, Mordecai would be walkin' back and forth outside the women's court, tryna get updates on how Esther was doin'.
2.12: Now the way this worked, each girl had to go through a whole year of beauty prep before she could even see the king—six months with myrrh oil, and six months with perfumes and all kinds of treatments.
2.13: After that, each girl got to bring whatever she wanted with her from the women's house to the king's place.
2.14: She'd spend the night with the king, but in the morning, she had to go to a different section where the concubines stayed, under Shaashgaz, the eunuch in charge of them. She wouldn't see the king again unless he asked for her by name.
2.15: When it was Esther's turn—she was the daughter of Abihail, Mordecai's uncle, who raised her—she ain't ask for nothin' extra. She just trusted what Hegai, the eunuch, suggested. And everybody who saw her? Fell in love with her instantly.
2.16: So they brought Esther to the king in his palace, in the tenth month (Tebeth), during the seventh year of his reign.
2.17: And the king? Man, he was gone. He loved Esther more than all the other women. She had that favor on her. So he put the crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti.
2.18: Then the king threw a huge party—The Feast of Esther—for all his officials and servants. He declared a holiday across the provinces and started blessin' folks with royal gifts.
2.19: Later on, when the virgins got gathered up again, Mordecai was sittin' at the king's gate.
2.20: Esther still hadn't told anybody she was Jewish or who her people were—just like Mordecai told her. She always listened to him, just like when she was growin' up.
2.21: Now one day while Mordecai was chillin' at the king's gate, he overheard two of the king's eunuchs—Bigthan and Teresh—plottin'. They were mad and tryna take the king out.
2.22: Mordecai found out and told Queen Esther. She went and told the king, makin' sure to say it came from Mordecai.
2.23: They looked into it, and yup—it was true. So they had both of those men hanged on the gallows. And it all got written down in the official royal records right in front of the king.

3.1: After all that, King Ahasuerus gave Haman—a descendant of Hammedatha the Agagite—a big promotion. Put him above all the other princes and leaders.
3.2: Everybody workin' at the king's gate bowed down to Haman like they was told. But Mordecai? Nah, he wasn't goin'. He ain't bow and he ain't show Haman no honor.
3.3: So the king's servants at the gate pressed Mordecai like, 'Why you disobeyin' the king's orders?'
3.4: They kept botherin' him about it, day after day, and he still wasn't budgin'. He told 'em straight up, 'I'm a Jew.' So they went and snitched to Haman to see if Mordecai's stance was really legit.
3.5: When Haman saw with his own eyes that Mordecai wasn't bowin' or showin' no respect, he got tight—dude was furious.
3.6: But he ain't wanna just deal with Mordecai alone. Once he found out Mordecai's people were Jewish, he set his sights on all of 'em. Haman was plottin' to wipe out every Jew in the whole kingdom.
3.7: In the first month, Nisan, of King Ahasuerus' twelfth year, they rolled dice (they called it 'Pur') to figure out the date for this evil plan. The lot landed on the twelfth month—Adar.
3.8: Then Haman went to the king like, 'There's a group of people scattered all over your kingdom. They different. They don't live like everybody else and they don't follow your rules. They a problem, for real.'
3.9: 'If it's cool with you, let's write up a law to get rid of 'em. I'll drop ten thousand talents of silver on whoever handle it and make sure it ends up in your treasury.'
3.10: The king took off his ring—the one with the royal seal—and gave it to Haman, son of Hammedatha the Agagite. That man was the Jews' #1 enemy.
3.11: Then the king told Haman, 'The money and the people—do what you want. It's in your hands now.'
3.12: On the thirteenth day of the first month, the royal scribes got to work. They wrote up Haman's orders and sent 'em to the king's governors, leaders, and officials in every province. The letter was written in every language and sealed with the king's ring.
3.13: The letters went out fast—sent by couriers across the kingdom—sayin' to kill, destroy, and wipe out every Jew, no matter the age, from kids to elders, women too. It was all supposed to go down in one day: the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar. And they could take whatever the Jews owned too.
3.14: Copies of the order were posted in every province so the people could get ready. That day was comin', and everybody had to know.
3.15: The couriers took off, movin' fast by the king's command. The decree was also announced in Shushan. Meanwhile, the king and Haman sat down drinkin' like it was nothin'. But the whole city of Shushan? Confused and shook.

4.1: When Mordecai heard everything that had gone down, he tore his clothes, threw on some sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the city cryin' loud and deep from the gut.
4.2: He walked all the way up to the king's gate, but couldn't go in, 'cause you ain't allowed inside the gate rockin' sackcloth.
4.3: Everywhere the king's decree showed up, the Jews were in full mourning. Folks was fastin', cryin', hollerin', laid out in sackcloth and ashes.
4.4: Esther's girls and eunuchs came and told her what was up, and it messed her up bad. She sent fresh clothes to Mordecai, tryna get him out that sackcloth—but he said nah, he wasn't takin' 'em.
4.5: So Esther called for Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs assigned to her, and told him to go find out what was really goin' on with Mordecai.
4.6: Hathach went out to meet Mordecai in the city square, right outside the king's gate.
4.7: Mordecai broke it all down for him—everything that happened and how Haman promised to drop big money into the king's account to wipe out the Jews.
4.8: He even gave Hathach a copy of the order posted in Shushan that said the Jews were gettin' destroyed. He told him, 'Show this to Esther. Make sure she gets it. Tell her she gotta go to the king and beg for her people.'
4.9: Hathach came back and told Esther exactly what Mordecai said.
4.10: Then Esther sent a message back to Mordecai through Hathach.
4.11: 'Everybody knows—man or woman—if you walk up in the king's inner court without bein' called, you dead. That's the law. Unless he stretches out that golden scepter. And me? I ain't been called in thirty days.'
4.12: So they took that message back to Mordecai.
4.13: Mordecai replied, 'Don't get it twisted—just 'cause you in the palace don't mean you safe. You not gon' escape what's comin' to the rest of us.'
4.14: 'If you keep quiet right now, help gon' come from somewhere else, but you and your fam? Y'all gon' be gone. But maybe—just maybe—you was made queen for this exact moment.'
4.15: Then Esther sent back her answer to Mordecai.
4.16: 'Tell all the Jews in Shushan to fast for me. No food, no drink—for three whole days and nights. Me and my girls gon' do the same. Then I'ma go see the king—even though it's against the law. And if I die… I die.'
4.17: So Mordecai left and did everything Esther told him to do.

5.1: On the third day, Esther got dressed in her royal fit and went to stand in the inner court of the king's palace, right across from where the king was sittin' on his throne, facin' the entrance.
5.2: When the king saw Queen Esther standin' there, she caught his eye—he was feelin' her. He reached out the golden scepter in his hand toward her. Esther stepped up and touched the tip of it.
5.3: The king said, 'What's up, Queen Esther? What you want? Whatever you ask—up to half the kingdom—I got you.'
5.4: Esther said, 'If it's cool with you, I'd love for you and Haman to come to a banquet I put together for y'all—today.'
5.5: The king said, 'Bet. Go get Haman right now so we can do what Esther said.' So both the king and Haman rolled through to the banquet Esther had set up.
5.6: While they sipped wine, the king asked again, 'Alright Esther, what's your ask? What's your request? Whatever it is—even up to half the kingdom—it's yours.'
5.7: Esther said, 'Okay, here's what I'm askin'—'
5.8: 'If I'm really in your good graces, and you're willin' to hear me out and make it happen, then come back tomorrow to another banquet I'm preparin' for you and Haman. Then I'll tell you exactly what I want.'
5.9: Haman left that day feelin' himself—real happy, real proud. But when he saw Mordecai sittin' at the king's gate not standin' up, not even flinchin', all that joy turned into rage.
5.10: Still, he held it together. Went home, called up his people and his wife Zeresh to vent.
5.11: He started braggin'—talkin' about how rich he was, how many kids he had, how the king kept promotin' him and puttin' him above everybody else in the kingdom.
5.12: Then he said, 'And on top of all that, Queen Esther ain't invite nobody but me to dine with her and the king. And guess what—she invited me again tomorrow.'
5.13: 'But none of it even hits right as long as I gotta see Mordecai the Jew sittin' there like he don't see me.'
5.14: His wife Zeresh and his friends told him, 'You know what? Build a gallows—make it fifty cubits high. First thing in the morning, ask the king to hang Mordecai on it. Then go enjoy that banquet with the king.' That idea sounded perfect to Haman. So he had the gallows built.

6.1: That night, the king couldn't sleep. So he told somebody to bring him the book of records—the royal chronicles—and they started readin' it out loud to him.
6.2: That's when they came across the part where Mordecai had snitched on Bigthana and Teresh—two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the doors. They had been plottin' to kill the king.
6.3: The king said, 'Wait—did we ever do anything to honor Mordecai for that?' The servants said, 'Nah, not a thing.'
6.4: The king said, 'Who's out there in the court right now?' At that exact moment, Haman had just walked into the outer court, ready to suggest hangin' Mordecai on the gallows he built.
6.5: The servants said, 'Haman's out there standin' in the court.' The king said, 'Bring him in.'
6.6: Haman came in, and the king asked, 'What should be done for the man the king wants to honor?' Now Haman? He was in his own head like, 'Who else would the king wanna honor but me?'
6.7: So Haman answered, 'For the man the king wanna honor—'
6.8: 'Bring out a royal robe the king himself has worn, and a horse the king's actually ridden—with the royal crest on its head.'
6.9: 'Then pick one of the king's top officials to dress him up and put him on that horse. Parade him through the city square, shoutin', "This what's done for the man the king wanna honor!"'
6.10: The king said, 'Bet. Go do all that—for Mordecai the Jew who sits at the gate. Don't skip nothin' you just said.'
6.11: So Haman had to grab the robe and the horse, dress Mordecai up, and walk him through the city square yellin', 'This how the king honors somebody!'
6.12: After that, Mordecai just went back to sittin' at the king's gate. But Haman? He ran home with his head down, grievin' hard.
6.13: He told Zeresh and all his friends everything that happened. His crew and his wife were like, 'If Mordecai's one of them Jews, and you already slippin', it's a wrap. You not gon' win this. You definitely gon' fall.'
6.14: While they were still talkin', the king's eunuchs showed up and rushed Haman off to the banquet Esther had prepared.

7.1: So the king and Haman pulled up to eat with Queen Esther.
7.2: On the second day, while they was sippin' wine, the king asked again, 'What you want, Queen Esther? Whatever your request is—even up to half the kingdom—I'ma make it happen.'
7.3: Queen Esther said, 'If I got favor with you, and if you really rock with me, then please—spare my life. And spare my people too. That's what I'm beggin' for.'
7.4: 'Me and my people—we been sold out. Somebody out here tryin' to destroy us, kill us off completely. If it was just about bein' sold into slavery, I wouldn't have said nothin'. But this right here? This ain't something the king should just take as a loss.'
7.5: King Ahasuerus snapped: 'Who did this?! Where he at?! Who got the nerve to pull somethin' like this?!'
7.6: Esther said, 'It's him—the enemy is this evil Haman!' And just like that, Haman's whole face dropped—he was shook in front of the king and queen.
7.7: The king got up, heated, and stormed out into the palace garden. Haman stayed behind beggin' Queen Esther for his life. He knew the king had already decided his fate, and it wasn't lookin' good.
7.8: When the king came back from the garden, he walked in and saw Haman fallin' all over the couch where Esther was sittin'. The king said, 'Oh, so now you tryna come at the queen too? Right here in my house?!' As soon as those words left his mouth, the guards came through and covered Haman's face.
7.9: Then Harbonah, one of the king's eunuchs, spoke up: 'Ayo king—look! There's a gallows fifty cubits high standin' at Haman's house. He built it for Mordecai—the same one who saved your life.' The king said, 'Hang him on it.'
7.10: So they hanged Haman on the very gallows he built for Mordecai. After that, the king finally cooled off.

8.1: That same day, King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther everything that used to belong to Haman, the Jews' enemy. And Mordecai got brought before the king 'cause Esther had finally told him how they was related.
8.2: The king took off his signet ring—the one he had taken from Haman—and gave it to Mordecai. Then Esther made Mordecai the boss over everything that used to be Haman's.
8.3: But Esther wasn't done. She fell at the king's feet, cryin', beggin' him to shut down Haman's evil plan—the one he made to wipe out the Jews.
8.4: The king stretched out that golden scepter toward her again. So Esther got up and stood before him.
8.5: She said, 'If it pleases the king, and if I still got favor in your eyes, and if this feels right to you—please cancel out those letters Haman wrote. The ones that ordered my people—the Jews—to be destroyed in every province.'
8.6: 'How can I just stand by and watch my people go through that? I can't sit back while they get wiped out.'
8.7: Then King Ahasuerus told Esther and Mordecai, 'Look, I already gave you Haman's house. And we hung him up 'cause he tried to lay hands on the Jews.'
8.8: 'Now y'all go write whatever you want to protect your people. Write it in my name, seal it with my ring—'cause once something's written in the king's name and sealed, it can't be taken back.'
8.9: So the royal scribes got called in that same day—in the third month, Sivan, on the twenty-third day. Mordecai dictated the letter to the Jews, all the governors, princes, and leaders from India to Ethiopia—127 provinces. They wrote it in every language and script, including the Jews' own.
8.10: Mordecai wrote it in King Ahasuerus' name, sealed it with the king's ring, and sent it out fast on royal horses bred for speed.
8.11: The letters gave the Jews permission to link up and defend themselves—to fight back, kill, and destroy anybody who came for them, no matter the age or gender—and they could take the enemies' goods too.
8.12: It was all set to go down on one day—the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar—across every province of the king's empire.
8.13: Copies of the new law got posted everywhere so the Jews could get ready to clap back and handle anybody comin' for them.
8.14: The royal messengers hopped on them fast horses and flew out with the orders, movin' quick 'cause the king ain't play about it. The decree was also put up in Shushan.
8.15: Mordecai came out from the king's presence lookin' like royalty—rockin' blue and white threads, a big gold crown, and a fine linen and purple robe. And Shushan? The whole city turned up.
8.16: The Jews were lit—full of joy, honor, and celebration.
8.17: In every city and province where the king's new order hit, the Jews threw feasts, celebrated hard, and had holidays. And a whole bunch of other folks started claimin' they were Jews too—'cause now they were scared of 'em.

9.1: In the twelfth month, the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day, the day came when the king's command and Haman's decree were supposed to go down. The enemies of the Jews thought they had it in the bag—but it flipped. The Jews rose up and handled those who hated them.
9.2: The Jews came together in their cities across all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to defend themselves and put hands on anyone tryna harm them. And nobody could stand against them—everybody was shook.
9.3: All the king's officials, satraps, governors, and workers were helpin' the Jews now—'cause they was scared of Mordecai.
9.4: Mordecai was big time now. He had clout in the palace and was known all over. Dude just kept risin'.
9.5: So the Jews came out swingin'—takin' down every single enemy with swords, no mercy, no hesitation. They did what they had to do to those who hated them.
9.6: In Shushan, the Jews killed five hundred men.
9.7: They also took out Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
9.10: The ten sons of Haman, the son of Hammedatha, the Jews' enemy. But they ain't touch nobody's stuff—they left the plunder alone.
9.11: That same day, word got back to the king about how many folks got handled in Shushan.
9.12: The king told Esther, 'The Jews killed five hundred men here in Shushan, plus Haman's ten sons. Imagine what they did everywhere else! So what you want now, Queen Esther? You got it.'
9.13: Esther said, 'If it's alright with you, let the Jews in Shushan run it back tomorrow just like today. And hang Haman's ten sons on the gallows too.'
9.14: The king said, 'Do it.' So they issued the order in Shushan and hanged all ten of Haman's sons.
9.15: The Jews in Shushan linked up again on the fourteenth day of Adar and took out three hundred more men. Still didn't touch the plunder.
9.16: Across the rest of the empire, the other Jews defended themselves, found peace from their enemies, and took out seventy-five thousand folks—but still didn't lay a finger on the loot.
9.17: That all happened on the thirteenth day of Adar. On the fourteenth, they chilled, threw a feast, and celebrated.
9.18: But the Jews in Shushan fought on both the thirteenth and fourteenth, so they rested and partied on the fifteenth.
9.19: That's why the Jews in small towns, in unwalled villages, celebrate the fourteenth of Adar with joy, food, and gift-givin'.
9.20: Mordecai wrote everything down and sent letters to Jews all over—from the closest to the farthest provinces.
9.21: He told them to lock in those two days every year—the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar—as days to celebrate.
9.22: They were the days when the Jews caught a break, when their sorrow turned into joy, and their pain turned into a holiday. Days to feast, celebrate, send gifts to each other, and bless the poor.
9.23: The Jews agreed to it and made it official—just like Mordecai wrote.
9.24: See, Haman the Agagite—enemy of the Jews—had plotted to wipe 'em out and had cast Pur (the lot) to destroy them completely.
9.25: But when Esther came to the king, he flipped the script and ordered that Haman's own evil plan fall back on him—and had him and his sons hanged.
9.26: That's why they called it Purim, after the word Pur. Because of what went down, what they saw, and how it all turned out.
9.27: The Jews made it law for themselves, their kids, and anyone who joined them—these two days had to be celebrated every year, without fail.
9.28: Every generation, every family, every province, every city—Purim had to be remembered. Nobody could let this tradition die out.
9.29: Queen Esther, daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote another letter to seal the deal on Purim with full authority.
9.30: Mordecai sent out peace-filled, truth-telling letters to all 127 provinces in the kingdom.
9.31: He confirmed the Purim celebration on its set days, just like he and Esther had laid it out—along with the traditions around fasting and grieving.
9.32: Esther's decree made everything official, and it got written down in the records.

10.1: King Ahasuerus laid down taxes across the whole land—even the islands out in the sea.
10.2: Everything that king did—his power, his strength, and how high he elevated Mordecai—it's all written down in the royal history books of Media and Persia.
10.3: Mordecai the Jew was second-in-command right under King Ahasuerus. He was a real one—respected by the Jews, loved by the people. He stayed lookin' out for his folks and always spoke peace over his people.
